title: Week 5 - UML & Design Principles
content: ## UML A common design language used to describe the structure and the behavior of software systems. Primarily used for: - helping devs communicate - requirements analysis, specification and design - generating code with tools ### Class Diagrams Has three sections: 1. class name 2. attributes 3. operations 1. if method has a return value add a colon after the closing parenthesis followed by the return type. - This diagram is missing the visibility of attributes and operations Attributes and operations should also have their class visibility reflected before their name. Levels are as follows: - `+` for public - `-` for private - `#` for protected ### Relationships **Association vs Aggregation** Association means these objects are related somehow whereas aggregation means this object is made up of these parts. **Composition** Not class composition (the design principle). When the parts cannot exist without the whole, like rooms in a house. **Generalization** For child parent relationships, the parent is the generalized version of a child. ## Sequence Diagram Describes the flow of logic in one particular scenario. The time sequence of the objects participating in the interaction. ## Statechart Diagram Describes the state changes of an object. There are three main components: 1. State: Represents the current condition of an object 2. Transition: Shows that an object switches state 3. Event: Triggers a transition # SOLID ## Single Responsibility Principle ## Open Closed Principle Software entities should be open for extension but closed for modification. **Closed for Modification**: To add new features we should not have to modify existing code **Open for Extension**: We should be able to add new features to a software component Following OCP makes it easy to add new features. Adhering to it often requires decoupling, which in turn, automatically follows SRP. - SOLID principles are intertwined and interdependent - SOLID principles are more effective when combined together ## Liskov Substitution Principle Objects should be replaceable with their subtypes without affecting the correctness of the program. **Advantages**: - Code that adheres to LSP is loosely dependent to each other and encourages code reusability - Code that does not adhere to LSP is tightly coupled and creates unnecessary entanglements ## Interface Segregation Principle No client should be forced to depend on methods it doesn't use. To find violations: - Fat interfaces with a large number of methods - Low cohesion where different methods in the same interface have entirely different function ## Dependency Inversion Principle High-level modules (business logic) should not depend on low-level modules (implementation details); both must depend on abstractions.
